phonemes.desc: Voiceless sibilant [s] plus short high back vowel [u]; in the Quechua two-syllable word the stress falls on this first syllable.
Bilabial stop [p] plus the diphthong [ai] written -ay; the final glide closes the name the way Quechua orthography writes it.

pronunciation.approximation: SOO-pie — two syllables, stress on the first; the '-ay' is the 'y' of 'fly'.

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: supay, 'spirit, demon' — the common noun González Holguín glosses as 'diablo' in his 1608 Vocabulario de la lengua general de todo el Perú

kin.label: Aymara
kin.form: supaya, the parallel Aymara word for a spirit of the dead or demon (Bertonio, Vocabulario de la lengua aymará, 1612)

kin.label: Colonial equation
kin.form: Spanish chroniclers equated Supay with the Christian Devil; Polo de Ondegardo (1571) reports the Inca dead descending to uku pacha in the power of the being they called Supay

pronunciation.note: Supay is Tier 2: the Quechua name carries no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII loses; only the capital distinguishes the restored form. Its pre-conquest meaning was 'spirit'; the modern sense 'devil' is a colonial redefinition, not an original one.

domains.title: Supay
domains.subtitle: Underworld
domains.lead: Supay is the lord of uku pacha, the inner world beneath the Andes — the domain of the dead, of cave-dwelling spirits, and of the mineral wealth the earth conceals. No temple bore his name; he was propitiated, not praised. Under Spanish rule the name was reforged: supay became the Quechua word for 'devil', and the lord of the inner world survives today as the miners' Tío.

cards.name: Lord of Uku Pacha
cards.desc: Master of the inner world beneath the earth where the dead dwell and the ore veins run (Polo de Ondegardo 1571; Cobo, Historia 13.10).

cards.name: Master of the Supaykuna
cards.desc: The dangerous spirits — the supaykuna — who send illness and haunt caves and crossroads; offerings kept them from taking the living.

cards.name: The Caves of Tambillos
cards.desc: Caverns near Huarochirí where the people said the supay dwelt; the Huarochirí manuscript records the rites paid there.

cards.name: The Miners' Tío
cards.desc: In the colonial mines, above all Potosí, miners fed the underground lord coca, alcohol, and cigarettes under the alias El Tío.

symbols.name: Cave mouth or mine shaft
symbols.meaning: The visible entrance to uku pacha; every shaft sunk into the earth is a doorway into Supay's jurisdiction

symbols.name: Coca and chicha
symbols.meaning: The standard offerings that made the underground lord generous toward the living who disturbed his realm

symbols.name: Funerary goods
symbols.meaning: Food, tools, and treasure interred with the dead as provision for the journey down to Supay's household

symbols.name: The horned devil figure
symbols.meaning: The post-conquest iconography in which the extirpation campaigns re-imagined Supay as the Christian Devil

mythology.lead: No Inca myth cycle of Supay survives on its own terms. Everything we know comes through colonial chroniclers, Quechua-language manuscripts, and the living memory of Andean communities — the record of a lord of the inner world who was propitiated, feared, demonized, and finally renamed, yet never quite dethroned.

myths.title: Lord of Uku Pacha
myths.text: The earliest European witness is the corregidor Polo de Ondegardo, whose 1571 report De los errores y supersticiones de los indios explains Inca cosmology as three stacked worlds: hanaq pacha, the upper world; kay pacha, this present world; and uku pacha, the inner world within the earth. The dead descended to uku pacha, Polo reports, and there remained in the power of the being they called Supay. Bernabé Cobo repeats the scheme a century later (Historia del Nuevo Mundo 13.10), adding that the dead were furnished with food, tools, and treasure for the journey down. Nowhere in these accounts is Supay a god of a temple or a priesthood: he is the one who holds the dead, and the offerings made at funerals are essentially payments that keep him from reaching further into the world of the living. The Inca underworld was not a place of punishment but of retention, and Supay was its jailer as much as its king. The belief encodes a sober arithmetic: every death adds to his household, so the living must forever feed the boundary between the worlds.

myths.title: The Caves of Tambillos
myths.text: The Quechua-language Huarochirí manuscript, recorded by the extirpator Francisco de Ávila in the first years of the seventeenth century (trans. Salomon & Urioste, 1991), treats supay not as a single lord but as a class of dangerous beings — the supaykuna — who dwell in caves, springs, hills, and crossroads and send illness to those who offend them. The most famous haunt is the cavern of Tambillos, near San Pedro de Huarochirí, where the people made offerings of coca and maize beer so that the spirits of the rock would not take their children. Scholars have long debated whether the chroniclers' single 'Supay, lord of the inner world' is a Spanish simplification of this older, plural spirit-world, or whether the supaykuna were always understood as the lord's subjects. The manuscript itself does not resolve the question; it simply shows communities negotiating, offering, and appeasing. Whatever the hierarchy, the logic is constant: the earth's interior is populated, and it must be paid. Supay's power was never worshipped from a temple — it was managed at the cave mouth, one offering at a time.

myths.title: Supay Becomes the Devil
myths.text: The most consequential chapter of Supay's history was written not by his believers but by his enemies. To convert the Andes, the missionaries needed Satan to have a local name, and they chose Supay's. González Holguín's Quechua Vocabulario (1608) glosses supay plainly as 'devil', and Pablo José de Arriaga's manual for destroying idolatry, the Extirpación de la idolatría (1621), names Supay as the demon who still receives the offerings poured at the Indian shrines. The campaign worked as language policy: within a generation Quechua speakers used supay for the Christian devil, and the pre-conquest meaning — 'spirit' — survived only in scholarly memory. Every colonial confession, sermon, and catechism pressed the word deeper into its new meaning. The transformation is a case study in conversion by redefinition: the church did not first destroy the lord of the inner world; it renamed him, and let the new name do the slow work of displacement. That the word, not the being, was conquered is proven by the mines, where the lord returned under another alias.

myths.title: El Tío of Potosí
myths.text: In the silver mines of the colonial Andes, above all at Potosí, miners developed the cult of El Tío, 'the Uncle': an effigy seated at the deepest level of each mine, fed coca leaves, cane alcohol, and cigarettes on Tuesdays and Fridays, and honored with the ch'alla libation. Michael Taussig's The Devil and Commodity Fetishism in South America (1980) connected the Tío to the older Supay of uku pacha — the lord of the inner world now ruling a new and terrible wealth. The miners said it plainly: the metal belongs to the one below, and he will trade safety for tribute; fatal accidents were read as unpaid debts. Unlike the church's Supay, this underground lord was negotiated with, not merely feared — a business partner who could be generous and could be cheated, at one's peril. The tradition continues today at Cerro Rico and in the Diablada dances of Oruro. Supay's late history shows a power outliving its own demonization: renamed the Devil by the conquerors, he remained — under a new alias — the actual master of the underworld the miners worked in.

lore.syncretism: Supay's entire afterlife is a history of forced translations. The conquering church mapped him onto Satan, and the mapping was so successful that modern Quechua and Aymara use supay as the ordinary word for devil. Yet the older figure survived the translation in the mines, where El Tío — the Uncle — continues the uku pacha lord's contract with those who take wealth from below. Scholars such as Taussig (1980) and Tristan Platt have read this double life as the emblem of colonial capitalism: the indigenous underworld lord re-employed as the owner of the silver that fed Europe. The Diablada dance traditions of Oruro and the miner rites at Potosí keep both identities visible at once — Christian devil masks performing unmistakably pre-Christian obligations.
lore.culturalLegacy: Supay remains embedded in Andean language itself: to this day supay means devil in Quechua and Aymara, a living fossil of the extirpation campaigns. In the mining regions of Bolivia the Tío effigies are still fed and still feared, and the Diablada festivals stage his masked dance before crowds of thousands. For scholarship, Supay is a key witness to how colonialism rewrote indigenous cosmology — studied by Taussig, Platt, and Duviols as the paradigmatic case of a deity demonized, renamed, and secretly retained. The name also circulates in global culture: Andean diaspora communities, museum exhibitions on Inca religion, and contemporary indigenous revival movements all return to the older, pre-Christian meaning of the word — spirit, not devil — as part of recovering what the extirpations tried to erase.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Supay is the lord of the underground who was renamed but never dethroned. Colonial priests thought that calling him 'devil' would finish him; instead the name became a mask, and behind the mask the old contract continued in the dark of the mines. There is a lesson in the economics of belief here: a power that controls what you need — passage for your dead, safety for your labor, metal for your markets — cannot be argued away. It can only be paid.

The restoration of Supay is therefore more than philological courtesy. It returns to the figure his own name, before the extirpators rewrote it, and it asks the reader to hold both histories at once: the lord of uku pacha and the colonial devil, the cave offerings and the Tuesday cigarettes at Cerro Rico. The earth, this name insists, keeps its own accounts, and its oldest creditor is still collecting.
lore.archaeology: No temple of Supay is known — he was propitiated at cave mouths, springs, graves, and mine faces rather than in built sanctuaries. The material record is therefore indirect: the rock shelters and cave shrines of the Huarochirí region, including Tambillos, where colonial extirpation records describe offerings of coca and maize beer; colonial-era dictionaries and confessionals that fixed supay as 'devil' (González Holguín 1608; Bertonio 1612); the Tío effigies and their offerings still maintained at Potosí and Olmillos; and the abundant documentary archive of the extirpation campaigns (Arriaga 1621; Duviols). The evidence honestly shows a cult of place rather than of monuments.
